title: A cold package-manager install on Linux creates a tree of files that each appear empty first, and truncates the manifest it was given

provenance.evidence: Twelve changes over the run. Every created file is seen at size 0 before it is seen with content: node_modules/dep/i.js at inode 550265 appears at 0 then reaches 18; package.json at inode 550268 appears at 0 then 47; package-lock.json at 550269 appears at 0 then 444; node_modules/.package-lock.json at 550270 appears at 0 then 317. The manifest the caller already had, package.json at inode 550260, is TRUNCATED IN PLACE: 34 -> 0 -> 71. Captured by tests/compatibility/save-patterns/v0/capture.mjs with a locally packed tarball, so the run needs no network.
blind_spots: open, flush, fsync and close are invisible to polling
a file created and removed inside one reading is invisible — a package manager's temporary staging is the likeliest thing this method misses

objects.role: package.json, the caller's own manifest — one identity, truncated through zero and rewritten

folder.fidelity: a backend that does not declare ObserveDurableBoundary
folder.omission_note: Each created file's empty appearance may be missed if the write lands inside one reading — and missing it is the SAFE direction, because the empty appearance is exactly the state that must never be checkpointed. Sequence 3 is NOT omissible: it is the caller's existing manifest being truncated, and a backend that missed it would have no record that the file changed at all.

expected.meaningful_durable_change: The dependency is installed: node_modules holds it, both lock files describe it, and package.json names it. One durable change for one install — never one per file.
expected.forbidden_note: Four Closed candidates are offered and only the last is meaningful. Every earlier one is a partially-installed tree: sequence 7 in particular has a rewritten package.json naming a dependency whose lock files do not exist yet. Mount 5 and folder 3 are the manifest at length zero — the caller's OWN file, momentarily empty, in the middle of a command they would describe as additive.

notes: This is the pattern that most punishes a per-file or per-Closed trigger. Thirteen mount events, four legitimate Closed anchors, one meaningful point. A trigger that checkpointed on each Closed would produce four records of a broken tree and one of a working one, with nothing in the record to say which is which.

It agrees with the darwin capture on the shape that matters — everything appears empty first, and the caller's manifest is truncated in place — while being far smaller (12 changes against 12,225 over 5,662 paths). The small case is the one worth replaying; the large one is the one worth remembering when sizing a byte-budget trigger.
The `--offline` flag against a locally packed tarball is what lets this be replayed on a machine with the network off, which the corpus needs and a registry install could not give.
